beats.act: cold open
beats.narration_text: Jambo — this is Liam, in for Divyank. Five real databases all claim to do the same thing: find the nearest vectors, fast. They don't do it the same way, and the differences are exactly where production systems break. Let's take all five apart, side by side.

beats.act: Act I — How Each One Finds Your Vector
beats.narration_text: Five different answers to the same question. Pinecone runs a proprietary approximate index, tuned in-house. Weaviate, Qdrant, and Chroma all build on H-N-S-W, a layered navigable graph. Pgvector adds I-V-F-Flat or H-N-S-W as an index type inside Postgres — not a new engine, an extension.

show.event: chips snap in per database: Pinecone, Weaviate/Qdrant/Chroma, pgvector

items: Pinecone — proprietary approximate index
Weaviate / Qdrant / Chroma — HNSW graph variants
pgvector — IVFFlat or HNSW, as a Postgres index type
props.caption: same goal, five different index designs

beats.act: Act I — How Each One Finds Your Vector
beats.narration_text: Two ways to combine a filter with a vector search. Post-filter: run the nearest-neighbor search first, then throw out results that fail the filter. Pre-filter: restrict the candidate set to what passes the filter, before or during the graph search itself.

caption settles

layers.title: Pre-filter
layers.sub: restrict the candidate set during the search itself

props.caption: same filter, two very different guarantees

beats.act: Act I — How Each One Finds Your Vector
beats.narration_text: Where each one lands. Qdrant built its own H-N-S-W variant specifically to filter during traversal. Weaviate and Pinecone integrate filtering into the index for the same reason. Pgvector inherits Postgres's query planner — a real pre-filter, when the planner cooperates. Chroma's filtering is the simplest of the five.

beats.act: Act II — Who Else Is In Your Index
beats.narration_text: One building, many separate units, one shared foundation. That's the multitenancy question for a vector database: how many customers' data can share one index without ever leaking into each other's search results.

shot.prompt: real archival photo of a building with many windows -- illustrative of multitenancy, not a literal depiction. Already sourced, see media/A2-1.source.txt

show.event: treated plate; slow push up the building
serif label lands: 'many units, one shared foundation'

beats.act: Act II — Who Else Is In Your Index
beats.narration_text: Weaviate ships multi-tenant collections as a first-class feature. Qdrant isolates tenants through payload-based partitioning. Pinecone uses namespaces — a separate slice inside one index. Pgvector inherits Postgres's own mature multitenancy: row-level security, schema-per-tenant, decades of prior art. Chroma's story here is the thinnest of the five.

show.event: chips snap in, one per database's multitenancy approach

items: Weaviate — multi-tenant collections, first-class
Qdrant — payload-based tenant partitioning
Pinecone — namespaces inside one index
pgvector — Postgres RLS / schema-per-tenant
Chroma — the thinnest story of the five
props.caption: isolation, five different ways

beats.act: Act II — Who Else Is In Your Index
beats.narration_text: One shared index with a tenant filter on every query, or one index per tenant. Shared scales cheaper and isolates worse under a filtering bug. One-per-tenant isolates perfectly and gets expensive fast — thousands of tenants means thousands of indexes to keep warm.

beats.act: Act II — Who Else Is In Your Index
beats.narration_text: Same requirement — billions of vectors — two different ceilings. Pinecone, Weaviate, and Qdrant scale outward: shard the index, add nodes, keep growing. Pgvector scales the way Postgres scales — mostly vertically, on one instance, with read replicas doing the rest.

beats.act: Act II — Who Else Is In Your Index
beats.narration_text: Neither ceiling is a defect. One is a dedicated engine built to be sharded from day one. The other is a general-purpose database that happens to index vectors too — and inherits Postgres's whole operational maturity in exchange.

beats.act: Act III — What Breaks in Production
beats.narration_text: Pinecone: fully managed means fully locked in — no self-hosted escape hatch, and cost scales with usage you don't fully control. Weaviate: self-hosting it well is real operational work — schema design, resource tuning, a system to run. Pgvector: it's still Postgres underneath — ANN index builds and the recall-versus-speed tuning are ongoing work, not solved by the extension alone.

beats.act: Act III — What Breaks in Production
beats.narration_text: Qdrant: a younger ecosystem, a smaller community than the decade-old alternatives — fewer battle scars documented publicly. Chroma: built for simplicity first — the tradeoff shows up exactly when you need serious multi-tenant scale, which is the opposite of what it was designed for.

beats.act: Act IV — Pick One
beats.narration_text: Pinecone: production RAG at scale, when a team wants zero infrastructure to run. Weaviate: hybrid search that blends keywords and vectors in one query. Pgvector: a team already living in Postgres, unwilling to add a second database for one feature. Qdrant: filtered vector search where the filter is doing real work. Chroma: prototyping and small apps before anything needs to scale.

beats.act: verdict
beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Indexing gets the attention, but the filtering strategy — pre-filter during the search versus post-filter after it — is what actually determines whether a metadata-heavy query returns the right answer at all. Multitenancy and scalability are the same question twice: Pinecone, Weaviate, and Qdrant shard outward across machines, pgvector inherits Postgres's own ceiling, and Chroma's story is thinnest of the five. Every one of the five carries a real, named tradeoff — managed lock-in, self-hosting labor, or a design built for simplicity over multi-tenant scale — and none of it is a defect, just an honest constraint. And there's no universal winner: pick based on your actual workload — an existing Postgres stack, a hybrid-search need, filter-heavy queries, or zero-ops managed scale.
